citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The licensee fails to maintain a program of adequate veterinary care that includes appropriate methods to diagnose and
treat diseases and injuries for the following animals noticed by the licensee:
• A mostly black (Torti coat) rabbit has a swollen hairless area, about 1 inch in diameter, located below the left ear with tan
crusted scab like material attached over it. Per the licensee, the hairless area had been there for two weeks. When
touched, it oozed creamy white material.
• An adult emu is missing feathers over most of its left leg such that the skin is exposed over a large area extending over
halfway up its side, approximately 12 inches wide by 18-24 inches long. Per the licensee, the bird has appeared this way
for at least 5 days.
• A lamb is limping on its left front leg, not weight bearing on it when standing, and only used it for short steps when
walking on it. Per the licensee during the inspection and in conversation with both APHIS officials, this lamb was found
with an exposed bone at its left front leg over two months ago. The attending veterinarian was not contacted, and
therefore, no treatment was given. Since then, the licensee said it has healed and the lamb is moving with the herd and
eating and drinking well. The licensee attributed the limp to the previously exposed bone injury. APHIS officials did not
appreciate any exposed bone or wound to the leg.
Inappropriate methods to treat and control diseases may lead to unresolved medical issues and undue distress for the
animals. The licensee must consult with a veterinarian to obtain a treatment plan for the animals noted above, and then,
moving forward, in cooperation with his attending veterinarian, the licensee must develop appropriate methods to prevent,
control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries.
Correct by: 10/14/2026

citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
Daily observation of the rabbits to assess their health and well-being is not being done adequately, nor is there direct and
frequent communication with the attending veterinarian regarding their health problems. Most of the rabbits have health
issues that have not been noticed by the licensee, and therefore, have not been evaluated by a veterinarian.
Of the rabbits closely evaluated, at least five of the nine (two black torti colored rabbits, two grey rabbits, and one
brownish/gray one), all had crusty brown material present at the ear canal opening, in at least one ear, and most had both
ears affected. One rabbit was occasionally shaking its head (black torti color), and two others (one cream colored and one
grey) had an overall rough haircoat/unkempt appearance.
Failure to identify the pre-existing health issues and failing to maintain timely communication about those findings with the
attending veterinarian can lead to treatment delay, which may negatively impact the health and well-being of the animals.
Each exhibitor shall establish and maintain programs of adequate veterinary care that include daily observation of all
animals to assess their health and well-being as well as direct and frequent communication so that timely and accurate
information on problems of animal health, behavior, and well-being is conveyed to the attending veterinarian.

The current Record of Animals on hand (acquisition record and disposition records) is not up to date or complete. Since
the last routine inspection, the following has occurred:
• Two lemurs, a peacock, and one budgie have been born at the facility without their dates of birth recorded.
• Disposition of three rabbits, seven chickens, three pheasants, and one goat have not been recorded.
Accurate and complete acquisition and disposition records are necessary to allow for medical and legal tracking of the
animals. The facility shall ensure that it makes, keeps and maintains records which fully and correctly disclose the
following information concerning all exhibition animals: name and address of person from whom the animal was acquired,
their USDA license number or Driver's license number/state, the name and address of the disposition of the animal, the
date of acquisition and/or disposition, and the species of the animal. The records shall include any offspring born of any
animal while in his or her possession.

citations.desc: Access and inspection of records and property; submission of itineraries.
citations.narrative:
During the two days of the inspection process, the licensee did not stay with the inspectors throughout the entirety of the
inspection process.
The licensee made statements inferring that he was very busy, had a lot to do and limited time for the inspection process.
Upon arrival on the first afternoon at 3:50 pm, he initially stated he could let us in for only 30 min. He was informed the
inspection process would take more than 30 min and that he also needed to secure his bull camel for safety purposes for
the APHIS officials. He agreed to give officials and hour the first afternoon and once the camel was secured, he then
called the officials in. When inspectors began to inspect rabbits, they requested licensee assistance and he would not
come into the enclosure to assist in handling of the animals.
On day two of the inspection, the camel was secured but the licensee did not secure a young mule that followed the
officials around, was physically pushing on the officials, ears back and attempting to bite and kick. In the presence of
APHIS officials, the licensee mentioned that the mule could kick out. Several times the licensee would again step away
from the officials to prepare diets and clean during the inspection process and was not available to manage the mule to
ensure safety of the officials. The officials would then utilize their clip boards to create a physical barrier between the mule
and them.
Without the accompaniment of a responsible adult for the entirety of the inspection process, its difficult for APHIS officials
to perform inspection duties, including animal and facility assessment. For future inspections, aggressive animals must be
contained for the safety of the officials, and the licensee or a second responsible adult shall be made available to
accompany APHIS officials during the entirety of the inspection process.
Correct by: Oct 10, 2026

The current contingency plan lacks specific tasks and details related to identified emergencies. For example, evacuation
is listed in inclement weather but no further details on how to contain and move all species from the facility are written.
Further, escaped animals, loss of electrical power, feed and water supply disruptions, and road closures are all listed as
potential emergencies without details on how to address those identified emergencies. A complete written contingency
plan is required to help ensure animal health and well-being in the event of an emergency or disaster; without this tool,
animals may suffer illness, injury, or death due to unpreparedness. Correct by developing, documenting and ensuring the
written contingency plan includes the specific tasks required to be carried out in response to the identified emergencies to
include such topics as sources of backup food and water as well as sanitation, ventilation, transport for all species if
evacuating, bedding, and veterinary care, etc. Finally, a chain of command needs to be identified while also addressing
how response and recovery will be handled in terms of materials, resources, and training needed.

There is no documentation maintained to indicate that an annual review of the contingency plan has been completed
since 05/20/2024. The contingency plan must be reviewed by the facility on at least an annual basis to ensure that it
adequately addresses all required contingency-related criteria and that no updates or changes need to be made to the
plan such as changes made as a result of any recent unforeseen circumstances. The facility must maintain
documentation of their contingency plan annual reviews including documenting any amendments or changes made since
the previous year's review.

The primary enclosure for nine rabbits is not being maintained in good repair to contain the rabbits or protect them from
injury. Per the licensee, since the last inspection one young rabbit has escaped the enclosure and was never recovered.
The young rabbits have escaped before but, per the licensee, usually return but this one was never found. Rabbits that
escape are at risk of injury or death. Primary enclosures shall be structurally sound and maintained in good repair to
protect the rabbits from injury, to contain them, and to keep predators out.

Housekeeping inside the rabbit enclosure needs to be addressed for the safety of the rabbits. The rabbit enclosure
housing nine rabbits has trash and miscellaneous items that do not pertain to the husbandry of the rabbits. These items
include an inversion table, an unused wire enclosure down on its side, a broken ceramic figurine and a broken upside
planter. These items need to be removed for the safety of the animals and to promote good housekeeping practices.
Premises (buildings and grounds) shall be kept clean and in good repair in order to protect the animals from injury and to
facilitate the prescribed husbandry practices set forth in this subpart. Premises shall remain free of accumulations of
trash.
Correct by: Oct 17, 2026

The facility does not have enough employees to maintain an acceptable level of care for the nine rabbits at this facility.
The licensee stated that he has no employees and it is only himself that cares for the rabbits at the facility. Based on the
number of non-compliant items detailed in the report pertaining to this subpart, including an inability to recognize vet care
issues with the rabbits’ ears, a mass on one rabbit that needed care and cleaning and maintaining the enclosure in good
repair, one employee is not sufficient and needs to be addressed.
A sufficient number of employees shall be utilized to maintain the prescribed level of husbandry practices set forth in this
subpart.
Correct by: Nov 9, 2026

The outdoor portion of the sheltered primary enclosures for the lemurs have areas of disrepair and they do not contain the
animals securely in their intended enclosures. The enclosure is divided to separate the adult males from the females and
their offspring. The bottom of the shared wire fence of the primary enclosures separating the males and females is not
secured allowing the juveniles, who are smaller, to enter the males’ side of the enclosure and also return to the females.
Juvenile lemurs were observed moving between the two enclosures during the inspection.
A lemur may injure itself or get a body part caught in the unsecured wire or be housed with potentially incompatible cage
mates.
Housing facilities for nonhuman primates must be designed and constructed so they are structurally sound for the species
of nonhuman primates in them. They must be kept in good repair, and they must protect the animals from injury while also
containing them securely.
Correct by: 10/20/2026

The perimeter fence around the sheltered enclosure for seven ring tail lemurs was insufficient in many areas. The
perimeter fence was constructed of 6-foot-tall wire mesh secured by 6-foot-tall metal T posts that, per the licensee, his
camel in the pasture surrounding this enclosure pushes and leans on, which continues to create multiple bowed in areas
towards the lemur’s outdoor portion of their sheltered enclosure. The height varied but reached a low of 59 inches in many
areas due to the fence being pushed in and/or down along three sides of the perimeter fence, excluding the back side
facing the neighboring property. Also, many areas of the wire mesh of the fence have been stretched and bent such that
large gaps were created between the wires, approximately 10 inches high by about 10 inches wide as observed starting
at the bottom of the fence to approximately 2 feet up from the ground. The lack of an adequate perimeter fence presents a
safety risk to the animals within the facility due to an inadequate secondary containment system to hold animals that may
escape their primary enclosures, or a sufficient barrier to keep animals and unauthorized persons out. The facility must
ensure that the nonhuman primates being housed in enclosures that are enclosed by an adequate perimeter fence, 6-feet
tall, that is constructed so that it restricts unauthorized humans, and animals the size of dogs, skunks, and raccoons from
going through it or under it and having contact with the nonhuman primates. The perimeter fence must be effective,
continuous, and at least 3 feet in distance from the primary enclosures unless a variance is obtained and approved by the
Administrator.

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
Housekeeping in the lemur enclosure needs to be addressed for both groups of animals.
* The enclosure side housing two males has an overgrowth of weeds throughout the area and a wooden shelter structure
on the ground in disrepair with a broken roof that has fallen into the shelter at approximately a 45-degree angle exposing
a broken support board that had broken in half, creating sharp points with a nail sticking out the end, approximately 1 inch
long.
*The female side with the two offspring has a large plastic M&M structure with a tray on top that is broken and cracked in
many areas creating multiple sharp points.
Weed growth prevents adequate cleaning of the enclosure, reduces visibility of the animals when they are on the ground
and can provide a living area for pests. Broken furniture items in the enclosure have the potential to cause injury and need
to be removed to keep the area clean and in good repair for the safety of the lemurs.
Premises where housing facilities are located must be kept clean and in good repair in order to protect the nonhuman
primates from injury, to facilitate the husbandry practices required in this subpart, and to reduce or eliminate breeding and
living areas for rodents, pests, and vermin. Premises must be kept free of accumulations of trash, junk, waste, and
discarded matter. Weeds, grass, and bushes must be controlled so as to facilitate cleaning of the premises and pest
control.
Correct by: Oct 22, 2026

The facility does not have enough adequately trained employees to maintain an acceptable level of husbandry practices
and care for the seven Ring-tail lemurs at this facility. The licensee stated that he has no employees and it is only himself
that cares for the lemurs at the facility. Based on the number of non- compliant items detailed in the report pertaining to
this subpart, including an inability to shift and contain lemurs for cleaning and feeding practices, maintain the perimeter
fence around the lemurs, address housekeeping issues inside the enclosure and maintain separation of the two groups,
one employee is not sufficient and needs to be addressed. Additionally, despite the length of time the licensee has
maintained lemurs, the licensee is not adequately trained to manage a group of lemurs, is not able to identify the sex of
the offspring even though they are off mom and has signs of being physically injured by the animals.
Every person subject to the Animal Welfare regulations maintaining nonhuman primates must have enough employees to
carry out the level of husbandry practices and care required in this subpart. The employees who provide husbandry
practices and care, or handle nonhuman primates, must be trained and supervised by an individual who has the
knowledge, background, and experience in proper husbandry and care of nonhuman primates to supervise others.
Correct by: Nov 9, 2026

Housekeeping needs to be addressed in the main large yard housing goats, sheep, alpaca and a camel. There are
various items that are in a state of disrepair left in the area like a broken picnic table with exposed nails, broken wire
enclosures, an old tractor, and broken feed bins. Additionally, the designated perimeter fence for the lemur enclosure and
primary fence for the birds is contained in this yard and shows signs of disrepair by animals pressing into the fencing
which has sharp points. These items and damaged fencing could cause a potential injury to the various hoofstock species
and need to be addressed to keep the area clean and in good repair.
Premises shall be kept clean and in good repair in order to protect the animals from injury and to facilitate the prescribed
husbandry practices set forth in this subpart. Accumulations of trash shall be placed in designated areas and cleared as
necessary to protect the health of the animals.
Correct by: Oct 18, 2026

The facility does not have enough adequately trained employees to maintain an acceptable level of husbandry practices
and care for the 19 hoofstock at the facility, including various species of sheep, goats, camel and alpaca. The licensee
stated that he has no employees and it is only himself that cares for the hoofstock at the facility. Based on the number of
non-compliant items detailed in the report pertaining to this subpart, and subparts covering vet care, records, and
contingency plans, one employee is not sufficient and needs to be addressed.
A sufficient number of adequately trained employees shall be utilized to maintain the professionally acceptable level of
husbandry practices set forth in this subpart. Such practices shall be under a supervisor who has a background in animal
care.
Correct by: Nov 9, 2026

Several sections in various aviary and pens housing birds are in disrepair and need to be addressed for the safety and
containment of the birds.
* In the emu enclosure, the top portion of mesh covering the shelter has some significant gaps between two sections of
chicken wire mesh. Other portions of the fencing around the Emu at the ground are bent and turned upward also creating
gaps and protruding up into the enclosure. The wire along the front of the Emu enclosure is stretched out and pulled
together with zip ties but there are still large gaps in the fencing.
*In the outdoor section of the parrot enclosure, there is a rusted metal ring attached to the side of the enclosure that
needs to be addressed. This ring is not an appropriate perch for the birds in this aviary and the rust that is flaking off can
be a potential hazard to the birds.
*The parrot indoor enclosure does not have wire mesh secured to a frame on the ground and the parrots are chewing the
wood baseboard around of the enclosure and there are some broken wires at the bottom of the enclosure.
*The aviary housing the poultry have several sections of the enclosure that are in disrepair with broken wires and a
shelter structure that is in disrepair with one whole side of the shelter appearing damaged.
Housing facilities for birds that are not in good repair may cause harm, discomfort, or injury to the birds. Housing facilities
for birds must be kept in good repair, protect the birds from injury, and restrict other animals from entering.

Five emus in their primary outdoor enclosure do not have adequate shelter provided to accommodate all five birds at one
time from inclement weather. The single shelter provided was a three-sided wooden structure, partially roofed, making the
under-roof area approximately 6 x 6 x 6 feet high. Two large plastic trash bins and another large bucket are also stored
within this roofed structure along the left side which decreases the amount of floor space available for the birds to
approximately 4 x 6 x 6 feet high. The trash bins provide food to the one emu who is choosing to be separated from the
group due to incompatibility thus increasing a need for additional shelter so all the birds can be comfortable out of the
elements if desired.
Outdoor housing facilities must provide adequate shelter for the local climatic conditions including direct sunlight,
precipitation, and wind. Shelter must also be constructed to provide sufficient space to comfortably hold all of the birds at
the same time, including birds that are low in the hierarchy, without adverse intraspecific aggression or grouping of
incompatible birds.

The facility does not have enough employees to maintain an acceptable level of care for the 49 birds at this facility. The
licensee stated that he has no employees and it is only himself that cares for the birds at the facility. Based on the number
of non-compliant items detailed in the report pertaining to this subpart, including an inability to manage compatibility
issues with the emu, maintain cleanliness for indoor enclosures and keep enclosures in good repair, a single employee is
not sufficient and needs to be addressed.
The facility must have a sufficient number of adequately trained employees or attendants utilized to maintain the
professionally acceptable level of husbandry and handling practices set forth in this subpart.
Correct by: Nov 9, 2026

The current grouping of five Emus is not compatible. One emu has extensive feather loss along the left thigh and leg, and
this bird was observed both days in the shelter area with its face to the corner wall. The emu eats and drinks in the shelter
and when it came out of the shelter, another bird began to chase and peck at it, until it went back under the shelter.
Birds may not be housed with other animals, including members of their own species, unless they are compatible, do not
prevent access to food, water, or shelter by individual animals, and are not known to be hazardous to the health and well-
being of each other. Compatibility must be determined in accordance with generally accepted professional practices and
by actual observations to ensure that the birds are, in fact, compatible.
Correct by: Oct 17, 2026

3.160(b) 
   
Compatibility and separation 
The current grouping of five Emus is not compatible. One emu has extensive feather loss along the left thigh and leg, and 
this bird was observed both days in the shelter area with its face to the corner wall. The emu eats and drinks in the shelter 
and when it came out of the shelter, another bird began to chase and peck at it, until it went back under the shelter.  
 
Birds may not be housed with other animals, including members of their own species, unless they are compatible, do not 
prevent access to food, water, or shelter by individual animals, and are not known to be hazardous to the health and well-
being of each other. Compatibility must be determined in accordance with generally accepted professional practices and 
by actual observations to ensure that the birds are, in fact, compatible.
